top.headline: Trump's $1.4 Billion in Crypto Earnings Is Becoming a Midterm Issue
top.blurb: Trump's financial disclosures show he has earned more than $1.4 billion from crypto ventures, including the $TRUMP meme coin and World Liberty Financial, the firm he co-founded with his sons. A new Financial Times/Focaldata poll finds 69% of voters, including nearly half his own 2024 supporters, worried about corruption or self-dealing in his second term, and corruption-themed ads now account for roughly $500 million in midterm spending.

top.headline: The FBI Anti-Corruption Squad That Was Investigating Susan Collins — Until Trump's DOJ Shut It Down
top.blurb: ProPublica reports the FBI opened a pay-to-play investigation into Sen. Susan Collins's dealings with defense contractor Navatek in 2024, after the firm's former CEO alleged campaign donations were traded for federal funding — an account records partly corroborated. The probe was shut down after Trump returned to office and purged the agents and prosecutors running it; Collins's office denies wrongdoing.

top.headline: Virginia's Top Democratic Redistricting Architect Indicted on Racketeering Charges Weeks Before the Midterms
top.blurb: State Sen. Louise Lucas, the 82-year-old Democrat who led Virginia's redistricting push, was charged with racketeering, money laundering and drug trafficking over an alleged marijuana enterprise. Democrats call it political payback timed to the midterms and her redistricting role; Attorney General Todd Blanche denies it, while Gov. Spanberger says the timing breaks the DOJ's own precedent against major actions near elections.

top.headline: Karnataka's Final Voter Rolls Lose Nearly 1 Crore Names After SIR
top.blurb: Karnataka's final electoral rolls fell from 5.5 crore to 4.5 crore voters, a drop of nearly 1 crore names — about 17.9% — after the state's Special Intensive Revision, with 8.6 lakh names later reinstated on appeal. Nationwide protests have demanded the Chief Election Commissioner's resignation over the revision's toll on genuine voters.

top.headline: Calcutta High Court Blocks Sharing of Documentary Alleging Modi-Adani Ties
top.blurb: The Calcutta High Court barred publishing or sharing 'The Friendship Files: How Modi and Adani Stole India', a 36-minute documentary alleging close ties between the two men, until January 31. The order came after Adani Enterprises filed a ₹50 crore defamation suit against entrepreneur Sabeer Bhatia and others involved in making it.

top.headline: Legacy Media Warns India's Data Law Enables 'Pre-Censorship'; Supreme Court Issues Notice
top.blurb: The Digital News Publishers Association, representing 21 mainstream outlets' digital arms, told the Supreme Court that India's personal data law has no journalism exemption, letting investigation subjects demand consent or erasure before publication — a power the group calls 'pre-censorship.' The Court issued notice on the petition without ruling on its merits.

top.headline: Israel Election Exit Polls Show Dead Heat, Leaving Netanyahu's Fate Uncertain
top.blurb: Exit polls in Israel's election show Netanyahu's coalition and the main opposition alliance each projected to win 51 of 120 seats, with Arab parties securing 18 — short of the 61 needed to govern either way. It is the first national election since the Hamas-led attacks of October 7, 2023, with turnout high and Netanyahu's hold on power now uncertain.

top.headline: Iran Holds Firm on Sanctions Relief and Hormuz Leverage as US Escalation Looms
top.blurb: Iran is maintaining its demands for sanctions relief, an end to the US naval blockade and guarantees against renewed attacks, even as regional diplomacy tries to head off escalation. Tehran's stance is shaped by distrust since June's collapsed memorandum, confidence in its leverage over Strait of Hormuz shipping, and a wait-and-see approach to the US midterms and Israel's election.

top.headline: Sudan's War Has Pushed 8 Million Children Out of School
top.blurb: UNICEF estimates 8 million of Sudan's 17 million school-age children are out of school since the civil war began in April 2023, with nearly half the country's school buildings no longer usable as classrooms. Aid groups warn the losses are pushing children into labour, early marriage and recruitment by armed groups, particularly girls.

top.headline: Abhishek Sharma's 113 Seals India's T20I Series Win Over New Zealand
top.blurb: India chased down New Zealand's 198/3 in just 13.2 overs in Wellington, with Abhishek Sharma blazing a 38-ball century studded with 13 sixes and Vaibhav Sooryavanshi adding 45. The six-wicket win gives India an unassailable 3-0 lead in the five-match series, with the fourth T20I in Auckland on October 30.

top.headline: 'Libby de Liberdade' Revisits the Goa Freedom Fighter Who Broadcast the Underground Resistance
top.blurb: Anjali Monteiro and KP Jayasankar's documentary centres on extended interviews with Libia Lobo Sardesai, now 102, who reported for the underground Voice of Freedom radio station during Goa's struggle against Portuguese rule before helping found the Women's Cooperative Bank and the Goa College of Home Science. The 79-minute film was built around a mural marking her 2024 birth centenary.

bengal.headline: Bengal's CEO Office Filed 16 Lakh Appeals Against Voter Inclusion, EC Tells Supreme Court
bengal.blurb: West Bengal's Chief Electoral Officer's staff filed roughly 16.1 lakh appeals against voter inclusions during the SIR, the Election Commission told the Supreme Court, amid a petition questioning who approved them.

bengal.headline: Rape-Murder Suspect Shot Dead in Police Encounter Near Bangladesh Border
bengal.blurb: Prahlad Das, the chief suspect in the rape and killing of a 17-year-old girl in Gaighata, was shot dead by police during a crime-scene reconstruction near the India-Bangladesh border.

bengal.headline: Bengal's Paused Teacher Recruitment Interviews May Resume in November
bengal.blurb: Bengal's secondary and primary school recruitment boards expect to restart interviews paused after an OBC quota cut, including hiring for 13,421 primary posts starting in November's second week.

travel.headline: Lonely Planet's 2027 Travel List Picks Rabat, Quebec and Kenya's Tsavo Parks
travel.blurb: Lonely Planet's Best in Travel 2027 guide names 25 destinations and 25 experiences, from Morocco's capital Rabat and Kenya's Tsavo national parks to Quebec, New Mexico and Sweden's Skanör-Falsterbo coast.

travel.headline: A Three-Legged Leopard's 240km Trek Highlights the Caucasus's Last Big Cats
travel.blurb: Persian leopards persist in the Caucasus on the thinnest of margins — just three sightings in Georgia and ten in Armenia over 20 years — with one three-legged male believed to have travelled 240km after losing a limb to old landmines.

happy.headline: Botswana Awards an Honorary Doctorate to the 97-Year-Old Who Fought for the San's Right to Stay in the Kalahari
happy.blurb: Roy Sesana, 97, who spent decades fighting the eviction of San communities from Botswana's Central Kalahari, received an honorary doctorate as the president who once represented them in court now works to restore their land rights.

tech_top.headline: Discord Will Make Public Server Messages Searchable on the Web Starting Mid-December
tech_top.pm_note: A platform's decision to make opt-out, not opt-in, the default for exposing user content is a product and policy choice worth scrutinizing before copying it into your own roadmap.
tech_top.blurb: Discord says each 'Discoverable' public server will get its own web page from November 16, and starting mid-December, some public channel messages may surface in web search results. Admins choose which channels participate and members can opt out, but critics say posting in a public server never implied consent to have it indexed — or used to train AI models.

tech_top.headline: Flock's CEO Blamed Russian Bots for the Backlash Against His Surveillance Company. The Evidence Doesn't Hold Up.
tech_top.pm_note: When a vendor facing a real customer revolt reaches for an unfalsifiable explanation instead of the complaint itself, that's a signal about how it will respond to your own escalations later.
tech_top.blurb: 404 Media examined Flock CEO Garrett Langley's claim, made to police chiefs in leaked audio, that opposition to his automatic-license-plate-reader company is mostly fake and driven by paid Russian bots. The outlet finds no evidence for the claim, which echoes other unsubstantiated theories, while communities keep canceling Flock contracts over real, documented concerns.

tech_top.headline: Anthropic Details Early Drug-Discovery Work, Including an Acquisition That Reached Mouse Trials in 18 Months
tech_top.pm_note: A one-person biotech reaching promising animal results in 18 months by using an AI model to coordinate contracts, logistics and 11 external labs previews how small a 'company' can get before AI makes headcount optional.
tech_top.blurb: Anthropic describes six deep-research partnerships using Claude for molecule design, manufacturing documentation and trial planning, plus its acquisition of Mithril Medicine — a one-person company whose founder used Claude to coordinate contracts and experiments across 11 external labs, reaching promising mouse results for a rare muscular dystrophy treatment in under 18 months.

tech_more.headline: Apple's $2,000 Foldable iPhone Duo Is Already Showing a Crease — and Some Screens Are Cracking Along It
tech_more.blurb: Early buyers of Apple's foldable iPhone Duo report a visible crease down the screen's middle, with some units cracking along that line and others showing a white band of stuck pixels that iFixit suspects comes from the hinge.

tech_101.text: A setting that's turned on for everyone automatically, leaving it to each person to notice and switch it off — as opposed to an opt-in default, where nothing happens until you actively choose it. Discord's move to make public messages searchable uses the opt-out version.

Camera networks, like those Flock Safety sells to police departments, that photograph and log every passing vehicle's plate, time and location — building a searchable record of where cars, and the people driving them, have been, not just the ones linked to a crime.

science.headline: A Technician Cracked a 1,600-Year-Old Roman Glass Mystery
science.blurb: The Lycurgus Cup, a 4th-century Roman glass vessel in the British Museum, turns jade green in reflected light and ruby red when light passes through it, and no one had reproduced the effect until University of Sheffield technician Lisa Hollands developed a recipe believed to rely on tiny gold and silver nanoparticles. The findings could inform new photonic materials and glasses for storing radioactive waste.

science.headline: NASA's Asteroid-Hunting Telescope Gets Its Sunshade and Solar Power Online
science.blurb: Engineers finished integrating 864 solar cells, generating up to 2 kilowatts, onto the 20-foot sunshade for NASA's NEO Surveyor mission, which will block the Sun's glare so the infrared telescope can spot hazardous asteroids and comets lurking near the Sun's direction. The sunshade also keeps the telescope cool and supplies all of the spacecraft's power.

science.headline: A Laser Upgrade Lets Cryo-Electron Microscopes See Proteins They Used to Miss
science.blurb: UC Berkeley researchers added a high-power laser phase plate to a cryo-electron microscope, shifting the electron beam's phase to sharpen contrast enough to resolve proteins as small as 50 kilodaltons — far below what conventional cryo-EM can usually see. The team hopes the technique will eventually reveal how molecular machines work together inside living cells.

philosophy.headline: How Intuitions Actually Work
philosophy.blurb: Philosopher Marc Moffett argues intuitions — from a gut sense a stranger is dangerous to a philosopher's reaction to a thought experiment — function like perception: they present their content as simply actual, and that presentational quality, not some special intellectual feeling, is what lets them justify belief without appealing to further beliefs.

philosophy.headline: Does the Demand That Everything Be Explainable Lead to Panpsychism?
philosophy.blurb: If the principle of sufficient reason — the demand that everything have an intelligible explanation — is true, the essay argues, consciousness may have to be a fundamental feature of matter itself, closing the otherwise unexplained gap between non-conscious stuff and conscious minds. Mørch and Spinoza reach similar conclusions by different routes, though the author doubts the reasoning can fully succeed.

philosophy.headline: Reason Can't Tell You What to Care About
philosophy.blurb: Reason alone cannot create inherent worth, the philosopher argues — it can only refine the needs and commitments we already have. Value begins instead with felt need, especially recognizing other people's inner lives, and reason's job is to help that coexist with others who value differently, not to settle what's worth caring about.

philosophy_101.text: The idea that intuitions — gut senses as well as philosophers' reactions to thought experiments — don't feel like a special kind of thinking so much as a kind of perception: they present something as simply true, the way seeing a chair presents a chair, which is what lets them justify a belief on their own.

The view that consciousness isn't something that only switches on in brains, but a basic property of matter itself, present in some form everywhere — proposed partly to avoid having to explain how non-conscious stuff could ever give rise to conscious minds in the first place.
